claim: HDAC3 is critical for activation of murine peripheral CD4+ T cells.
source: Here, we show that histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) is critical for activation of murine peripheral CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells failed to proliferate after in vitro TCR/CD28 stimulation.
source: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells failed to proliferate and blast after in vitro TCR/CD28 stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells failed to blast after in vitro TCR/CD28 stimulation.
source: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells failed to proliferate and blast after in vitro TCR/CD28 stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Upon T-cell activation, genes involved in cholesterol biosynthesis are upregulated.
source: Upon T-cell activation, genes involved in cholesterol biosynthesis are upregulated while genes that promote cholesterol efflux are repressed.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5d.

claim: Upon T-cell activation, genes that promote cholesterol efflux are repressed.
source: Upon T-cell activation, genes involved in cholesterol biosynthesis are upregulated while genes that promote cholesterol efflux are repressed.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5e showing downregulation of Abca1 and Abcg1 in WT cells after activation.

claim: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells had reduced levels of cellular cholesterol both before and after activation.
source: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells had reduced levels of cellular cholesterol both before and after activation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Filipin III staining data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: HDAC3-deficient cells upregulate cholesterol synthesis appropriately after activation.
source: HDAC3-deficient cells upregulate cholesterol synthesis appropriately after activation, but fail to repress cholesterol efflux; notably, they overexpress cholesterol efflux transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 5d showing normal expression of cholesterol synthesis genes.

claim: HDAC3-deficient cells fail to repress cholesterol efflux after activation.
source: HDAC3-deficient cells upregulate cholesterol synthesis appropriately after activation, but fail to repress cholesterol efflux; notably, they overexpress cholesterol efflux transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 5e showing elevated Abca1 and Abcg1 expression.

claim: HDAC3-deficient cells overexpress cholesterol efflux transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1.
source: HDAC3-deficient cells upregulate cholesterol synthesis appropriately after activation, but fail to repress cholesterol efflux; notably, they overexpress cholesterol efflux transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 5e and RNA-Seq data in Figure 7a.

claim: Addition of exogenous cholesterol restored proliferative capacity of HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells.
source: Repression of these genes is the primary function for HDAC3 in peripheral CD4+ T cells, as addition of exogenous cholesterol restored proliferative capacity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6a showing restored proliferation with cholesterol supplementation.

claim: HDAC3 is essential during CD4+ T-cell activation to repress cholesterol efflux.
source: Collectively, these findings demonstrate HDAC3 is essential during CD4+ T-cell activation to repress cholesterol efflux.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: After activation, CD4+ T cells must pass through metabolic checkpoints to proliferate, differentiate, and generate robust immune responses.
source: After activation, CD4+ T cells must pass through a number of metabolic checkpoints in order to proliferate, differentiate, and generate robust immune responses.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Chapman et al., 2019; Chapman and Chi, 2018; Ron-Harel et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013.

claim: The metabolic transition after TCR engagement is characterized by cell growth, IL-2 signaling, increased anabolic metabolism, and reprogramming of mitochondrial metabolism.
source: This metabolic transition shortly after TCR engagement has been defined as quiescence exit, and is characterized by several key cellular events including cell growth, interleukin-2 (IL-2) signaling, increased anabolic metabolism, and reprogramming of mitochondrial metabolism (Chapman et al., 2019; Chapman and Chi, 2018; Ron-Harel et al., 2016; Tan et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Metabolic checkpoints prepare CD4+ T cells for proliferation by generating cellular building blocks such as fatty acids, sterols, nucleotides, and amino acids.
source: Each of these checkpoints prepares CD4+ T cells for proliferation and effector function by generating the cellular building blocks required for activated T cells such as fatty acids and sterols, nucleotides, amino acids, and other metabolites (Bensinger et al., 2008; Geiger et al., 2016; Johnson et al., 2018; Kidani et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2017; Ricciardi et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: mTORC1 directs many aspects of metabolic reprogramming after T-cell activation.
source: Mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), particularly mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1), directs many aspects of metabolic reprogramming after T-cell activation (Tan et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: mTORC1 drives lipid synthesis through the expression of sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBPs).
source: One role of mTORC1 is to drive lipid synthesis through the expression of sterol regulatory element-binding proteins (SREBPs) (Kidani et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: SREBPs are transcription factors that orchestrate lipid synthesis after T-cell activation.
source: SREBPs are transcription factors that orchestrate lipid synthesis after T-cell activation (DeBose-Boyd and Ye, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Recently activated T cells halt cholesterol efflux.
source: In addition to increasing lipid and sterol synthesis, recently activated T cells also halt cholesterol efflux (Bensinger et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Activated T cells rapidly decrease expression of cholesterol efflux transporters to retain recently generated cholesterol.
source: Activated T cells rapidly decrease expression of cholesterol efflux transporters in order to retain recently generated cholesterol (Michaels et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Both increased cholesterol synthesis and decreased cholesterol efflux are required for successful proliferation and blast formation.
source: Both of these steps, increased cholesterol synthesis and decreased cholesterol efflux, are required for successful proliferation and blast formation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to studies showing disruptions in these processes inhibit T cell activation.

claim: Disruptions in cholesterol synthesis in CD8+ T cells inhibited blasting and proliferation after TCR engagement.
source: Disruptions in cholesterol synthesis in CD8+ T cells inhibited blasting and proliferation after TCR engagement (Kidani et al., 2013), while enforced expression of cholesterol efflux transporter ABCG1 inhibited proliferation (Bensinger et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Enforced expression of cholesterol efflux transporter ABCG1 inhibited T cell proliferation.
source: Disruptions in cholesterol synthesis in CD8+ T cells inhibited blasting and proliferation after TCR engagement (Kidani et al., 2013), while enforced expression of cholesterol efflux transporter ABCG1 inhibited proliferation (Bensinger et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Deletion of ACAT1 enhanced proliferation and effector function in CD8+ T cells but not CD4+ T cells.
source: Cholesterol metabolism may not be identically regulated in CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, as deletion of Acetyl-CoA Acetyltransferase 1 (ACAT1) enhanced proliferation and effector function in CD8+ T cells but not CD4+ T cells (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: T cells require an optimal amount of cholesterol to exit quiescence.
source: Together, these studies point to an important 'cholesterol checkpoint' in which T cells require an optimal amount of cholesterol to exit quiescence.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a synthesis of cited studies.

claim: HDAC3 is a Class I HDAC that deacetylates lysine residues on histones H3 and H4 to repress gene expression.
source: Histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) is a Class I HDAC that deacetylates lysine residues on histones H3 and H4 in order to repress gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about HDAC3.

claim: HDAC3 serves as a targeted regulator of key gene expression during T-cell development.
source: Previously, our group has shown that HDAC3 serves as a targeted regulator of key gene expression during T-cell development.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: During positive selection in the thymus, HDAC3 is required for downregulation of RORγt.
source: During positive selection in the thymus, HDAC3 is required for downregulation of RORγt (Philips et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: HDAC3 suppression of P2RX7 is critical for survival of double positive thymocytes in the ATP-rich thymic cortex.
source: Further, HDAC3 suppression of the purinergic-receptor P2RX7 is critical for survival of double positive thymocytes in the ATP-rich thymic cortex (Philips et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: HDAC3 acts as an inhibitor of the cytotoxicity program of CD8+ T cells.
source: Recently, the role of HDAC3 as an inhibitor of the cytotoxicity program of CD8+ T cells was examined using E8I-Cre, which initiates deletion in CD8 SP thymocytes (Ellmeier et al., 1997; Tay et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: HDAC3 is a highly specific transcriptional regulator in lymphocytes.
source: Collectively, this work supports the idea that HDAC3 is a highly specific transcriptional regulator in lymphocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a synthesis of previous work.

claim: Adult dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice had normal numbers of naive and memory CD4+ T-cell populations in the spleen.
source: Adult dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice had normal numbers of naive and memory CD4+ T-cell populations in the spleen, but had a significant decrease in CD8+ T-cell populations (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Adult dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice had a significant decrease in CD8+ T-cell populations in the spleen.
source: Adult dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice had normal numbers of naive and memory CD4+ T-cell populations in the spleen, but had a significant decrease in CD8+ T-cell populations (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: HDAC3 is required for T-cell maturation, leading to a block at the recent thymic emigrant (RTE) stage.
source: Previous work in which HDAC3 was deleted in the thymus revealed HDAC3 is required for T-cell maturation, leading to a block at the recent thymic emigrant (RTE) stage (Hsu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: The CD8 SP population in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO thymus had a loss of HDAC3 protein level compared to WT CD8 SP.
source: Surprisingly, the CD8 SP population had a loss of HDAC3 protein level compared to WT CD8 SP (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO initiated deletion as early as the CD8 SP thymocyte stage.
source: Thus, dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO initiated deletion as early as the CD8 SP thymocyte stage.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the HDAC3 expression data in Figure 1b.

claim: HDAC3 expression was unaffected in CD4 SP thymocytes in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice.
source: HDAC3 expression was unaffected in CD4 SP thymocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Approximately 25% of RTEs were HDAC3 deficient in the dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO.
source: HDAC3 deletion began soon after T cells egress from the thymus since ~25% of RTEs were HDAC3 deficient in the dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: More than 75% of mature naive T cells (MNTs) were HDAC3 deficient in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice.
source: Further, MNTs were enriched for HDAC3− cells, with >75% of them being HDAC3 deficient (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Only 25% of memory CD4+ T cells were HDAC3 deficient in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice.
source: Surprisingly, only 25% of the memory CD4+ T cells were HDAC3 deficient (Figure 1c) suggesting that HDAC3-deficient memory CD4+ T cells had a competitive disadvantage to the HDAC3-sufficient memory CD4+ cells in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: HDAC3-deficient memory CD4+ T cells had a competitive disadvantage to HDAC3-sufficient memory CD4+ cells in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice.
source: Surprisingly, only 25% of the memory CD4+ T cells were HDAC3 deficient (Figure 1c) suggesting that HDAC3-deficient memory CD4+ T cells had a competitive disadvantage to the HDAC3-sufficient memory CD4+ cells in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the data in Figure 1c.

claim: There were very few HDAC3-deficient Th1, Th2, Th17, Treg, and Tfh cells in the spleen in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice compared to WT.
source: There were very few HDAC3-deficient T helper (Th) cells including Th1, Th2, Th17, Treg, and Tfh cells in the spleen in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice when compared to WT (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The frequency of HDAC3-deficient Th17 cells in the mesenteric lymph nodes was reduced in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice.
source: The frequency of HDAC3-deficient Th17 cells in the mesenteric lymph nodes (mLNs) was also reduced in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CD4-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice generated Th2, Th17, Treg, and Tfh cells at about the same frequency as WT cells in the spleen and mesenteric lymph node although total numbers were highly reduced.
source: CD4-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice generated Th2, Th17 and Treg and Tfh cells at about the same frequency as WT cells in the spleen and the mesenteric lymph node although total numbers were highly reduced (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: HDAC3-deficient cells could differentiate in a noncompetitive environment.
source: Of note, HDAC3-deficient cells could differentiate in a noncompetitive environment.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data from CD4-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice shown in Figure 2.

claim: HDAC3-deficient T cells from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice differentiated normally and expressed the transcription factors Foxp3, RORγt, GATA3, and T-bet under appropriate polarizing conditions.
source: Notably, HDAC3− T cells from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice differentiated normally and expressed the transcription factors Foxp3, RORγt, GATA3, and T-bet under appropriate polarizing conditions (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: HDAC3-deficient T cells from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice had a normal frequency of cells expressing IFN-γ, IL-4, and IL-17A under appropriate conditions.
source: Likewise, HDAC3− T cells from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice had a normal frequency of cells expressing IFN-γ, IL-4, and IL-17A under appropriate conditions and coexpression of each lineage-defining transcription factor and cytokine was observed for each Th lineage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: HDAC3 was not required for Th differentiation in vitro.
source: Thus, HDAC3 was not required for Th differentiation in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the in vitro differentiation assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: The total number of cells harvested from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice in the day 4 in vitro differentiation assay cultures was more than 4-fold lower than WT for Th1, Th2, and Th17 differentiation assays.
source: Interestingly, the total number of cells harvested from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice in the day 4 in vitro differentiation assay cultures was >4-fold lower than WT for each of the Th1, Th2, and Th17 differentiation assays (Figure 3, right).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: HDAC3-deficient T cells from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice had increased Foxp3 MFI in Treg differentiation assays.
source: The output of Foxp3+ Treg cells in the dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO culture was not statistically different than WT, and intriguingly, HDAC3− T cells from the dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice had increased Foxp3 MFI and a higher percentage of cells that were Foxp3+ among all cells in the culture (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells had a severe defect in their ability to proliferate upon CD3/CD28 stimulation.
source: There was a severe defect in the ability of HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells to proliferate upon CD3/CD28 stimulation (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by CFSE proliferation data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Greater than 80% of HDAC3-deficient T cells upregulated CD69 expression after CD3/CD28 stimulation.
source: Greater than 80% of HDAC3-deficient T cells upregulated CD69 expression, and the MFI was similar between WT and HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells, indicating that HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells can respond to TCR signals (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells can respond to TCR signals.
source: Greater than 80% of HDAC3-deficient T cells upregulated CD69 expression, and the MFI was similar between WT and HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells, indicating that HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells can respond to TCR signals (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of CD69 upregulation data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: IL-2 expression was reduced by 50% in HDAC3-deficient T cells compared to WT after αCD3/αCD28 stimulation.
source: However, IL-2 expression was reduced by 50 % in HDAC3-deficient T cells compared to WT after αCD3/αCD28 stimulation (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The percentage of HDAC3-deficient cells that induced CD25 expression 3 days after αCD3/αCD28 stimulation was greatly reduced.
source: In addition, the percentage of HDAC3− cells that induced CD25 expression 3 days after αCD3/αCD28 stimulation was greatly reduced (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Reduced expression of both IL-2 cytokine and IL-2 receptor likely contribute to defective proliferation in the HDAC3-deficient population.
source: Since IL-2R signaling plays a critical role in T-cell proliferation after TCR activation (Boyman and Sprent, 2012; Ross and Cantrell, 2018), reduced expression of both IL-2 cytokine and IL-2 receptor likely contribute to defective proliferation in the HDAC3− population.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the IL-2 and CD25 data, supported by citations.

claim: HDAC3-deficient T cells had a significant decrease in the percentage of viable cells compared to WT 24 hours after activation.
source: HDAC3-deficient T cells had a significant decrease in the percentage of viable cells compared to WT (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by viability dye data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells did not have a statistically significant change of P2RX7 expression in either naive or memory CD4+ T cells after CD3/CD28 stimulation.
source: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells did not have a statistically significant change of P2RX7 expression in either naive or memory CD4+ T cells (Figure 4f).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Deletion of HDAC3 in peripheral CD4+ T cells results in impaired proliferation and survival after activation.
source: Altogether, deletion of HDAC3 in peripheral CD4+ T cells results in impaired proliferation and survival after activation, suggesting that HDAC3 protein is necessary for successful expansion of CD4+ T-cell populations after TCR engagement.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a summary of findings from Figure 4.

claim: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice exhibited a comparable percentage of Egr2+ cells with WT CD4+ T cells 16 hours after αCD3/αCD28 stimulation.
source: Sixteen hours after αCD3/αCD28 stimulation, CD4+ HDAC3− T cells from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice exhibited a comparable percentage of Egr2+ cells with WT CD4+ T cells, but the MFI of HDAC3-deficient cells was significantly reduced (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The MFI of Egr2 in HDAC3-deficient cells was significantly reduced compared to WT 16 hours after αCD3/αCD28 stimulation.
source: Sixteen hours after αCD3/αCD28 stimulation, CD4+ HDAC3− T cells from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice exhibited a comparable percentage of Egr2+ cells with WT CD4+ T cells, but the MFI of HDAC3-deficient cells was significantly reduced (Figure 4g).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO CD4+ T cells had reduced phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6.
source: Additionally, dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO CD4+ T cells had reduced phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 (Figure 4h), indicating that mTOR activity was diminished in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: mTOR activity was diminished in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO cells.
source: Additionally, dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO CD4+ T cells had reduced phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 (Figure 4h), indicating that mTOR activity was diminished in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the p-S6 data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO CD4+ T cells had a decrease in both basal and maximal respiratory capacity compared to WT as measured by oxygen consumption rate.
source: The assay revealed the dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO CD4+ T cells had a decrease in both basal and maximal respiratory capacity compared to WT as measured by oxygen consumption rate (OCR) (Figure 4i).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Seahorse data shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Basal extracellular acidification rate was reduced in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO cells.
source: Moreover, basal extracellular acidification rate was also reduced in the dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO cells have a disruption in the metabolic reprogramming required for successful T-cell activation.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO cells have a disruption in the metabolic reprogramming required for successful T-cell activation.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the metabolic data in Figure 4.

claim: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice had a reduced frequency of blasting cells 3 days after αCD3/αCD28 stimulation.
source: Three days after αCD3/αCD28 stimulation, HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells had a reduced frequency of blasting cells, and their median size measured by forward scatter area (FSC-A) was significantly reduced compared to WT cells (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The median size of HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells measured by forward scatter area was significantly reduced compared to WT cells 3 days after αCD3/αCD28 stimulation.
source: Three days after αCD3/αCD28 stimulation, HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells had a reduced frequency of blasting cells, and their median size measured by forward scatter area (FSC-A) was significantly reduced compared to WT cells (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Granularity as measured by side scatter area was reduced in HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells 3 days after αCD3/αCD28 stimulation.
source: Granularity as measured by side scatter area (SSC-A) was also reduced in the HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Volume-adjusted Filipin III signal was significantly reduced in HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells both before and after a 20-hr stimulation with αCD3/αCD28.
source: Notably, volume-adjusted Filipin III signal was significantly reduced in HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells both before and after a 20-hr stimulation with αCD3/αCD28 (Figure 5b), indicating that cellular cholesterol concentrations were decreased in the absence of HDAC3.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Filipin III staining data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Cellular cholesterol concentrations were decreased in HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells.
source: Notably, volume-adjusted Filipin III signal was significantly reduced in HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells both before and after a 20-hr stimulation with αCD3/αCD28 (Figure 5b), indicating that cellular cholesterol concentrations were decreased in the absence of HDAC3.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the Filipin III data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: HDAC3-deficient T cells had a small but significant reduction in CTB fluorescence after 20 hr of αCD3/αCD28 stimulation.
source: After 20 hr of αCD3/αCD28 stimulation, HDAC3-deficient T cells had a small but significant reduction in CTB fluorescence, consistent with a reduction of lipid raft concentration (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by CTB staining data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: HDAC3-deficient T cells had a reduction of lipid raft concentration.
source: After 20 hr of αCD3/αCD28 stimulation, HDAC3-deficient T cells had a small but significant reduction in CTB fluorescence, consistent with a reduction of lipid raft concentration (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the CTB data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Srebf1 and Srebf2 showed similar expression between WT and HDAC3 cKO T cells before or after stimulation.
source: Srebf1 and Srebf2, genes that produce sterol response element-binding proteins and serve as key regulators of lipid synthesis (Bertolio et al., 2019) showed similar expression between WT and HDAC3 cKO T cells before or after stimulation (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Key genes involved in cholesterol synthesis and homeostasis such as Hmgcr, Dhcr7, Sult2b1, Abcc1, Idi1, and Sqle were all expressed normally in dLck-HDAC3 cKO cells.
source: In addition, key genes involved in cholesterol synthesis and homeostasis such as Hmgcr, Dhcr7, Sult2b1, Abcc1, Idi1, and Sqle were all expressed normally in dLck-HDAC3 cKO cells (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Expression of Nr1h2, which encodes Liver X Receptor Beta (LXRβ), showed normal expression in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO T cells.
source: Additionally, expression of Nr1h2, which encodes the protein Liver X Receptor Beta (LXRβ) and serves as a cholesterol sensitive transcription factor, also showed normal expression in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO T cells (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells had a higher Filipin III signal after TCR stimulation.
source: However, HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells had a higher Filipin III signal after TCR stimulation (Figure 5b), indicating they were still capable of increasing cholesterol synthesis despite reduced mTORC1 activation.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells were still capable of increasing cholesterol synthesis despite reduced mTORC1 activation.
source: However, HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells had a higher Filipin III signal after TCR stimulation (Figure 5b), indicating they were still capable of increasing cholesterol synthesis despite reduced mTORC1 activation.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the Filipin III data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: TCR/CD28 signaling in HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells is sufficient to drive the expression of cholesterol biosynthesis genes.
source: Collectively, these data indicate TCR/CD28 signaling in HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells is sufficient to drive the expression of cholesterol biosynthesis genes.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the gene expression data in Figure 5d.

claim: At baseline, mature naive CD4+ T cells from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice had a 3.4-fold increase in expression of Abcg1 transcripts compared to WT.
source: At baseline, mature naive CD4+ T cells from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice had a 3.4-fold increase in expression of Abcg1 transcripts and a 3.5-fold increase in Abca1 transcripts compared to WT (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: At baseline, mature naive CD4+ T cells from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice had a 3.5-fold increase in Abca1 transcripts compared to WT.
source: At baseline, mature naive CD4+ T cells from dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice had a 3.4-fold increase in expression of Abcg1 transcripts and a 3.5-fold increase in Abca1 transcripts compared to WT (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Twelve hours after activation, Abcg1 transcript expression in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice was 8.1-fold higher than WT activated T cells.
source: Twelve hours after activation, Abcg1 transcript expression in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice was 8.1-fold higher than WT activated T cells, while Abca1 transcript expression in the activated dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO was 7.1-fold higher than WT activated T cells (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Twelve hours after activation, Abca1 transcript expression in the activated dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO was 7.1-fold higher than WT activated T cells.
source: Twelve hours after activation, Abcg1 transcript expression in dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO mice was 8.1-fold higher than WT activated T cells, while Abca1 transcript expression in the activated dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO was 7.1-fold higher than WT activated T cells (Figure 5e).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells that received exogenous cholesterol proliferated equivalently to WT T cells.
source: Remarkably, HDAC3-deficient CD4+ T cells that received exogenous cholesterol proliferated equivalently to WT T cells (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by CFSE proliferation data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: HDAC3-deficient dLck-Cre HDAC3 cKO CD4+ T cells treated with cholesterol had a strong recovery in the percentage of blasting cells compared to WT.

claim: HDAC3 regulates cholesterol availability in CD4+ T cells.

claim: HDAC3 is required during T-cell activation to transcriptionally repress cholesterol efflux through ABCA1 and ABCG1.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that HDAC3 regulates cholesterol availability in CD4+ T cells and that HDAC3 is required during T-cell activation to transcriptionally repress cholesterol efflux through ABCA1 and ABCG1.

claim: T cells are uniquely sensitive to changes in cholesterol concentration shortly after activation.

claim: Genetic deletion of Abcg1 in CD4+ T cells results in increased proliferation.

evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Transcriptional control of genes involved in cholesterol availability is critical for successful T-cell responses.
